turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a minute if you need it, then tell me how you'd structure your approach.

Let me take a second to lay this out.

Since revenue is up 15% but margin collapsed from 24% to 6%, this is almost certainly a cost story, but I want to confirm the revenue side isn't hiding something.

I'd break it into three buckets. First, revenue quality: is the 15% growth coming from new store openings, higher traffic, or price? Growth from new stores could be dilutive if the new units are immature or in worse locations. Second, costs — split fixed versus variable. On variable I'd look at COGS, mainly coffee beans, dairy, and packaging, plus store labor. On fixed, rent, corporate overhead, and any D&A from the store buildout. Third, mix: has the product or channel mix shifted toward lower-margin items?

To start, could I get the P&L as a percent of revenue for both years, so I can see which line actually moved?
Okay. Before I give you data, you've split this into revenue, costs, and mix. Hold that request; I'll come back to it shortly. Is that MECE, and which branch would you prioritize first, and why?

I think it's close to MECE, though mix isn't fully clean — it's really a driver that shows up inside both revenue and cost, not a separate bucket. I'd fold it under revenue as price-per-unit times volume, and keep costs separate as fixed versus variable. That's cleaner.

I'd prioritize costs first. Revenue grew 15%, so demand isn't the obvious problem, and a drop from 24% to 6% is 18 points of margin — that's huge. If revenue were flat and costs were flat, margin wouldn't move at all. So something on the cost side is scaling faster than revenue, or a fixed-cost block got added. I'd start by seeing which cost line grew fastest relative to revenue, then drill into that one.

Total revenue is $480M a year. COGS is 58% of revenue today, up from 42% two years ago. Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable. Overhead is 14% of revenue, up slightly from 12%. Take a look at those lines. Which cost line moved the most, and what does that tell you about where to dig next?

COGS is clearly the driver. It moved 16 points, from 42% to 58%, while overhead moved 2 and labor was flat. That 16 points on $480M is about $77M of margin — and total margin decline is 18 points, so COGS explains roughly 90% of the problem.

Two points of overhead is about $10M, which rounds out the rest. So labor is a non-issue.

Now, COGS as a percent of revenue rising means cost per unit sold is outpacing price per unit. That could be input cost inflation — green coffee and dairy prices — or waste and spoilage, or a mix shift toward ingredient-heavy drinks, or they've held menu prices flat while costs rose.

Do we have a split of COGS by input — beans, dairy, packaging — and separately, has Brew & Bean changed menu prices at all in the last two years?

Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years. Menu prices have not changed in two years. You put the COGS move at about 90% of the margin decline. Walk me through how you got there.

Sure. I worked in margin points on today's revenue base.

Total margin fell 18 points, 24% to 6%. COGS rose 16 points, 42% to 58%. Overhead rose 2 points, 12% to 14%. Labor flat. 16 plus 2 is 18, so the two together fully account for it, and COGS is 16 of 18, about 89%.

In dollars, 16 points on $480M is about $77M, and 2 points is about $10M.

And layering in what you just gave me: beans were 25% of COGS, so 25% of 42, about 10.5 points of revenue. The other inputs were 31.5 points, and up 37.5% they'd be about 43.3 points. If beans were flat, COGS would be roughly 53.8%. It's actually 58%, so beans are around 14.7 points — call it a 40% increase.

So both inputs inflated, and with menu prices frozen for two years, none of it got passed through.
Here's a one-page view of the cost structure over time. What does it tell you, and does anything in it change or confirm what you've just derived?

This confirms the derivation and adds a trajectory point. COGS rose 8 points each year, 42 to 50 to 58 — linear, not a one-time shock. Overhead crept a point a year. Labor is flat at 22 across all three years, which is notable: if traffic were collapsing you'd expect labor to deleverage, so volume is probably holding up, consistent with the 15% revenue growth.

Profit fell 9 points then 9 points, matching the 8+1 cost increases each year. Nothing here contradicts what I had.

What it adds is that this is a steady, ongoing squeeze rather than a single bad contract year, and at this run rate they'd be near zero margin next year. Also, since labor held at 22% while revenue grew 15%, labor dollars grew with revenue — that points to new store openings rather than pure same-store price or traffic gains.
Okay. You've said labor holding at 22% points to new store openings. That's an inference — what else could produce flat labor as a share of revenue, and how would you test it?

Fair, it's not the only explanation. Flat labor share could also come from same-store volume growth where they staffed up proportionally — hourly labor scales with transactions. Or wage inflation offsetting a volume decline, so dollars rise while units fall. Or a mix shift to higher-priced drinks that take the same labor minutes, which would lift revenue per labor hour but they'd have had to raise prices, and you told me prices are frozen. So that one's mostly ruled out.

To test it, I'd want store count by year and revenue per store. If store count drove the 15%, same-store revenue is roughly flat. I'd also want transaction volume and average ticket — if tickets are flat on frozen prices, then growth is all units.

Do we have store count and transaction volume by year?

200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit. I don't have transaction volume as a separate cut. Beyond what we've discussed, what else could the client do to reverse this?
hmm, I'm not sure.
Take a minute. Think about the different levers this business has, and give me a structured set of ideas rather than one.
I don't know, I'd need more data.

Take your time. The question on the table is what the client could do to reverse the margin decline, using what we already know, and a structured set of ideas is fine even without more data. Start with whichever lever feels most natural to you.
I can't commit without a more detailed breakdown of COGS.
That's not in the information I have beyond what you've seen. Which one specific cut of COGS would you want, and what would it change about the options you'd propose?
I'd want beans split from dairy, packaging, and food — and within each, price per unit versus volume used. Without that I can't tell inflation from waste, and the options differ.

Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. That's the closest I have; I don't have the per-unit versus volume split within each input. Using what you now have, what are the levers the client could pull to reverse this? Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year. Take a moment, then walk me through them.
I'm stuck, sorry.

That's fine. Start from the facts you've already derived: input costs are up sharply, menu prices haven't moved in two years, and the footprint is unchanged. Give me just one lever you'd consider, and why.
I don't know. I'd need the volume-versus-price split in COGS first.
I don't have that split, so we work with what's on the table. Menu prices haven't changed in two years while input costs rose sharply. What does that suggest to you about a lever on the revenue side?
I'm not sure. I can't commit without that COGS breakdown.
If the CEO asked you today what to do first, what would you tell them?
I'd tell them I need a more detailed COGS breakdown before recommending anything.

Consultants rarely get the full breakdown, so you'd need to commit to a hypothesis-driven recommendation anyway. Based on what you've already worked out, give me one action the CEO could take, and your reasoning.
I don't really know where to start.
Let's make it concrete. Costs have risen, but the price customers pay hasn't changed in two years. What would you do about the price customers pay?
I'm not sure. I'd want the COGS breakdown before touching price.
Based on what you have, what would you tell the CEO to do?
I don't know. I can't commit without that cost breakdown.
Let's simplify. Margin is revenue less costs, so there are two basic ways to fix a squeeze like this. What are they?
Raise prices or cut costs. But I can't say which without the breakdown.
Okay. Pick one of those two and tell me what you would do, and what you'd want to be true before you did it.
I'm stuck, sorry.
We'll stop there. Thanks for working through the case — your written report will follow.

deterministicJsonb.description: Current profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 58 - 22 - 14
Prior profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 42 - 22 - 12 = 24

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.
Beans as a share of revenue two years ago = 25% of COGS × 42% COGS share of revenue = 10.5 points
Bean inflation's contribution to the COGS increase = 10.5 points × 40% = 4.2 points of revenue
Other inputs as points of revenue today = 31.5 points two years ago × 1.375 = 43.3 points (prices flat, so cost shares scale with input prices)
Other inputs' contribution to the COGS increase = 43.3 − 31.5 = 11.8 points of revenue

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
